paraphrase: One-on-one tutoring that adapts to each young child is reserved for the few; most kids learn reading and arithmetic without patient personal help.
Teams want small bespoke tools for their own workflows, and agents make them easy to build, but sharing and running them safely stays hard.
AI assistants are used alone in private chats, so teams cannot work together with agents the way they do in shared documents.
Three years into the AI shift, few new consumer products built on it have reached ordinary people beyond chat assistants.
Families already provide unpaid care for ageing relatives while caregivers are scarce and almost no technology is built for older people.
Most workers are not at desks, yet software for construction, maintenance and field crews has barely changed in two decades.
Cheap voice clones and deepfake video calls are fuelling fraud, and businesses lack reliable ways to prove someone is a real person.
Financial compliance is still stitched together with spreadsheets, siloed tools and costly staff, and grows harder in each new market.
Software makers ship breaking changes with little warning and customers miss changelogs, causing outages for teams that depend on them.
Farms depend on chemical pesticides that leave residues in food and water while pests and weeds keep adapting to them.
Most AI startups sell tools that help people do a job; few deliver the finished service itself at software-like cost.
Personal health data from tests and wearables rarely turns into individual, specific guidance for the person it describes.
Company know-how is scattered across heads, old email, chat threads and tickets, blocking automation and slowing newcomers.
Every user sees the same software interface regardless of their role or habits, so most software fits nobody especially well.
Hardware teams wait weeks for a new physical part where rivals in Shenzhen get one in a day, slowing every design loop.
Incumbent business software has grown bloated and pricey, leaving room for leaner challengers now that building software is cheaper.
AI agents increasingly browse, buy and update records, but they do it on software designed for humans clicking buttons.
Complex manufacturing supply chains are run on spreadsheets and phone calls, so firms cannot see disruptions beyond direct suppliers.
Most companies lose the knowledge from meetings, tickets and customer conversations because nothing captures and learns from it.
Teams have tools to write code fast but little help deciding what to build, which matters most and is still guesswork.
Agencies are hard to scale: margins are thin, work is manual and growth means hiring more people.
Stablecoins are becoming real payment rails, but the everyday financial services built on top of them are largely missing.
Domestic metal buyers wait eight to thirty weeks for rolled metal and often cannot buy direct from mills.
Skilled physical trades take years to learn, and workers on the job get little real-time guidance when they hit something unfamiliar.
Training language models remains painful, with broken SDKs and fragile tooling eating researchers' days.
There is a shortage of skilled tradespeople for building infrastructure, and retraining routes for displaced workers are slow.
Video generation is becoming cheap and realistic, yet few products turn it into something people use every day.
Small teams can now build big companies with little capital, but the tooling to run such lean operations is immature.
Firms buying AI tools still do the legal and professional work themselves; few companies sell the finished outcome directly.
Designers worried about AI replacing them rarely start companies, though shipping products has never been easier.
Customer phone calls still mean long holds and phone trees; people want a human because automated lines are so poor.
Despite decades of productivity apps, email piles up and tasks stay undone because tools track work rather than do it.
Roughly a third of healthcare spending goes to administration created by disconnected systems and paperwork.
A truly personalised tutor for every learner has been a dream for decades and is still out of reach for most students.
Teaching methods have barely changed in decades despite a huge education sector and over a billion students.
Home security relies on legacy companies whose features have not changed in years, while smarter systems stay in commercial buildings.
Employees repeat the same tedious parts of their jobs daily and lack an easy way to build their own automations.
Commuters waste drive time they could use to triage email and draft replies by voice.
Most people make poor decisions about saving, investing, debt and taxes, and good personal financial advice is costly.
Each AI app keeps its own memory of the user, and people cannot control what personal data each one sees.
Compliance and audit work means reading dense rules and cross-checking documents by hand, and costs keep rising.
Many business workflows still need a person clicking through websites and desktop apps that offer no other way in.
Personal help with errands, admin and planning has only been affordable for the wealthy.
Websites are built for human visitors while a growing share of traffic is software agents that must impersonate people.
Each industry has repetitive specialist workflows that general software never fits well.
Growing companies find ERP software expensive, painful to implement and hated by the staff who use it.
Large firms still process invoices, contracts and customer requests by hand in repetitive back offices.
Clinic staff are overworked and underpaid as owners and overheads take most of what they bill.
Much healthcare spending goes to middlemen rather than the people providing care, inflating costs for patients.
